# QR Symbology Architecture

Design record for supporting multiple QR symbologies, Standard QR (ISO/IEC 18004), Micro QR (ISO/IEC 18004), and rMQR (ISO/IEC 23941), in one library. This document defines how the codebase is organized so each symbology can be added without destabilizing the others. Implementation details live in code comments next to the code.

---

## What

### Symbology status

| Symbology | Standard | Encode | Matrix decode | Image decode |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Standard QR (versions 1–40) | ISO/IEC 18004 | Shipped | Shipped | Shipped (Tier 1–2) |
| Micro QR (M1–M4) | ISO/IEC 18004 | Shipped | Shipped | Shipped (Tier 1–2, conservative measured envelope) |
| rMQR (R7x43–R17x139) | ISO/IEC 23941 | Encode + render done (Phase 5, encoder MVT met; not yet released) | Done (Phase 6, decoder MVT matrix rows met; not yet released) | Done (Phase 7, Tier 1–2, measured envelope incl. keystone up to 4 % on R17x139; not yet released) |

### Document set

Specs are one set of files per symbology plus this cross-cutting record, see the [documentation index](../README.md) for the file list. Structure and naming rules live in [docs_authoring_guidelines.md](../docs_authoring_guidelines.md); new symbologies copy the section skeleton of the Standard QR document of the same type.

### Internal organization

Internals are split into shared primitives and per-symbology pipelines.

**Shared primitives** (`Internals`, `Internals.BinaryEncoders`, `Internals.BinaryDecoders`, `Internals.ImageDecoders`), knowledge that is identical across all three symbologies:

| Component | Why it is shared |
|---|---|
| `GaloisField`, `Polynom`, `EccBinaryEncoder`, `EccBinaryDecoder` | All three symbologies use Reed-Solomon over GF(256) with the same primitive polynomial (0x11D) |
| `BitWriter`, `BitReader` | Bit-stream packing is symbology-independent |
| `ModuleBitPacker` | Byte-per-module ↔ MSB-first bit-packed conversion of the Micro QR and rMQR data models (`SetCoreData` / `GetCoreData`) is the same operation for both; Standard QR's `QRCodeData` keeps its own (frozen) storage kernel |
| `ECCInfo` | RS block structure (data codewords, ECC per block, up to two block groups) describes all three symbologies |
| `BinaryInterleaver` | Block interleaving of data then ECC codewords depends only on the `ECCInfo` block structure; Standard QR and rMQR interleave identically (Micro QR has one block). Lifted from `Internals.StandardQR` to `Internals.BinaryEncoders` when rMQR became the second consumer (rMQR Phase 5.4); the only symbology-specific input, the remainder-bit count, is passed in by the caller |
| `EncodingMode`, `TextAnalyzer`, `CharacterSets` | Mode alphabet definitions (Numeric / Alphanumeric / Byte character classes, alphanumeric encoding values) are shared; only indicator widths and legality differ per symbology |
| `SegmentDecoders` | Segment payload bit groups (numeric 10/7/4, alphanumeric 11/6, byte 8·count), the byte-charset heuristics (UTF-8 validation, BOM, Latin-1 widening) and the ECI designator reader (lifted from `QRBinaryDecoder` when rMQR became its second consumer, Phase 6) are identical across symbologies; the mode/count indicator framing that differs stays in each symbology's bitstream decoder (lifted out of `QRBinaryDecoder` in Phase 3 when the second consumer appeared) |
| `LuminanceConverter`, `PixelLayout`, `PerspectiveTransform` | Image preprocessing and geometry are symbology-independent. The luminance kernels are the seam the first-party image adapter feeds (see the package seam below) |
| `Point`, `Rectangle` | Plain geometry types |
| `ModuleRunScanner`, `ModuleRunEnumerator<TView>` | Merging dark modules into horizontal runs depends only on the `IModuleMatrixView` shape, not the symbology. One implementation serves both the renderer's merged-run drawing path and the public `GetModuleRectangles` surface on all three data types, so the geometry the public API reports is by construction the geometry the renderer draws for an unstyled symbol (a styled one draws its finder as one pattern instead, which `GetModuleRectangles` still reports as the merged runs of its modules) |

**Per-symbology pipelines** (`Internals.StandardQR`, later `Internals.MicroQR`, `Internals.RmQR`), knowledge specific to one symbol format:

- Capacity / ECC / interleaving tables and version selection
- Mode indicator and character-count indicator widths
- Format (and version) information encoding and decoding
- Function pattern layout, data module placement, mask patterns and mask scoring
- Symbol detection and sampling in images

Dependency rule: shared code never references a symbology namespace; symbology namespaces never reference each other. Each symbology pipeline composes the shared primitives. Existing Standard QR code moves under `Internals.StandardQR` unchanged, no behavioral or algorithmic modification accompanies the move.

Two detection primitives were lifted from `Internals.StandardQR` to the shared `Internals.ImageDecoders` namespace when Micro QR image detection (Phase 4b) became their second consumer, exactly the trigger this document prescribed:

- `Binarizer.ComputeOtsuThreshold`, generic binarization (moved out of `QRImageDecoder`)
- `FinderPatternFinder`, the 1:1:3:1:1 run-ratio scan and cross-checks; Micro QR and rMQR use the same finder pattern shape (single finder instead of three) via `FindCandidates` (all cross-checked candidates), while Standard QR keeps its best-three selection in `TryFind`
- `FinderAxisEstimator`, single-finder local module scale and axis recovery (axis-aligned dark-light-dark runs, angular sweep), lifted from the Micro QR image decoder when rMQR image detection (Phase 7) became its second consumer; the Micro QR image benchmark stayed flat

### Package architecture

Since 2.0.0 the library ships as three NuGet packages built from two assemblies in this repository (the core split, 2026-09):

| Package | Assembly | Contents | Depends on |
|---|---|---|---|
| `FeatherQR` | `FeatherQR.dll` | Generators, decoders, data types, options, segmentation, `ModuleRect` geometry, the luminance kernels | Nothing on net8.0 and net10.0; `System.Memory` (netstandard2.0) and `System.Runtime.CompilerServices.Unsafe` (netstandard2.1) |
| `FeatherQR.SkiaSharp` | `FeatherQR.SkiaSharp.dll` | `SymbolRenderer`, the `SKCanvas` extensions, the image builders, `IconData` and shapes, `SKBitmap` decoding as extension members on the core decoders | `FeatherQR`, `SkiaSharp` |
| `SkiaSharp.QrCode` | none | An empty compatibility metapackage: the ID the library shipped under through 1.x keeps restoring | `FeatherQR.SkiaSharp` |

Namespaces follow the packages: `FeatherQR` and `FeatherQR.SkiaSharp`, with the internals of each under `FeatherQR.Internals` and `FeatherQR.SkiaSharp.Internals`. The former `SkiaSharp.QrCode.Image` sub-namespace is folded into `FeatherQR.SkiaSharp`; one namespace per package is the cheapest shape to explain in a major that changes every `using` line anyway.

**Dependency rules.**

- The core references no package that is not a BCL shim, and the shims only where the framework lacks `Span<T>`, `ArrayPool<T>` and `Unsafe`. Two guards hold this: `CoreAssemblyDependencyTest` reads the core assembly's references from metadata for every target framework, and `tools/check_package_deps.cs` reads the packed nuspecs (see "Package graph" below). A dependency that slips in passes build and test and fails both.
- The rendering package reaches the core through the public surface, plus the enumerated `InternalsVisibleTo` uses recorded below ("Package seam"). The core never references the rendering package.
- Skia types appear only in the rendering assembly. Inside `namespace FeatherQR.SkiaSharp` the simple name `SkiaSharp` binds to that namespace, so `using SkiaSharp;` sits above the file-scoped namespace declaration and qualified `SkiaSharp.SKBitmap` spellings are not used.
- No unified `Create(symbology, ...)` entry point is ever added. The three generators, decoders and data types do not reference each other, and that is what makes trimming precise: a consumer that uses one symbology keeps one symbology.

**What the split buys, measured.** With `PublishTrimmed` (`TrimMode=full`) on a console app, measured on 2026-09-04 on the pre-split assembly:

| Consumer profile | Trimmed managed assembly |
|---:|---:|
| QR encode only | 95 KB |
| All three symbologies, encode | 153 KB |
| All three, encode and decode, including `TryDecode(SKBitmap)` | 229 KB |
| Untrimmed net10.0 | 384 KB |

The managed assembly was never the cost. `libSkiaSharp` is 11.9 MB per RID, cannot be trimmed, and is deployed whether or not a single Skia call survives; only a package boundary removes it, and only for consumers that reference `FeatherQR` alone. A per-symbology package split was rejected: it would save untrimmed consumers roughly 100 to 130 KB, cost a four-package core with a public surface for the shared kernels, and buy nothing for trimmed consumers, who already get the numbers above.

**What "lightweight" means.** The brand word is defined as zero dependencies in the core, zero allocations on the hot paths, and trim and NativeAOT safety. It is not a claim about assembly bytes: at 300 to 390 KB the core is larger than single-symbology libraries because it carries three symbologies, the decoders and the SIMD tiers. The README states the definition in its first lines so the name never has to be defended against a byte count.

### Package seam: what the rendering package reaches through `InternalsVisibleTo`

`FeatherQR` grants `InternalsVisibleTo` to `FeatherQR.SkiaSharp`. The rule is that a third-party renderer must be writable against the public surface alone, so every internal the first-party renderer still uses is listed here with either its public replacement or the reason it stays internal. The list is checked by building the rendering project with the grant removed: whatever fails to compile is the list.

| Internal | Used by | Decision |
|---|---|---|
| `LuminanceConverter.Convert(pixels, width, height, rowBytes, PixelLayout, premultipliedAlpha, luminance)`, `PixelLayout`, `ImageDimensions.TryGetPixelCount` | `Internals.BitmapLuminanceConverter` and the `SKBitmap` decode overloads | **Stays internal, by decision (core split Phase 2).** The public decode seam is `TryDecodeImage(luminance, width, height, ...)`, which already lets a third-party adapter decode from any image library; what it does not get is the SIMD conversion and the white-compositing behavior for free, and no such adapter has been asked for. Publishing the kernels is a one-way door (removing an API needs a major, adding one needs a minor), so they stay internal until a concrete request exists. The `TryDecodeImage` documentation states the white-compositing expectation so a hand-written converter does not composite transparent pixels against black. The rendering package keeps a single-entry adapter, `FeatherQR.SkiaSharp.Internals.BitmapLuminanceConverter` (`SKColorType` to `PixelLayout` over `SKPixmap.GetPixelSpan()`), so promoting the seam later is a visibility change, not a redesign |
| `RmQRConstants.QuietZoneModules`, `RmQRConstants.IsValidVersion` | `RmQRCodeImageBuilder` | **Replaced.** The builder reads the specified quiet zone from `default(RmQRCodeGeneratorOptions).QuietZoneSize`, which is the same constant behind a public property, and validates a requested version with `Enum.IsDefined`, which the contiguous `RmQRVersion` enum makes exact |
| `IModuleMatrixView`, `StandardQrMatrixView` / `MicroQRMatrixView` / `RmQRMatrixView`, `ModuleRunEnumerator<TView>` | `SymbolRenderer` merged-run and per-module drawing loops | **Stays internal, by decision.** The public equivalent is `GetModuleRectangles` / `TryGetModuleRectangles` on the three data types, built on the same `ModuleRunScanner`, so a third-party renderer draws exactly the geometry the first-party one does. The first-party renderer keeps the streaming enumerator because it draws each run as it is found with no rectangle buffer; going through the public surface would add a `GetModuleRectanglesMaxCount()`-sized rental per render (up to ~15,700 rectangles for version 40) to the one path that is measured as allocation-free. Exposing the struct-generic view machinery itself would freeze an implementation detail as API for one caller |

### Package graph: what each nuspec declares

Three packages ship from one `dotnet pack` at one lockstep version (`Directory.Build.props`): `FeatherQR` (core), `FeatherQR.SkiaSharp` (rendering, depends on `FeatherQR` and `SkiaSharp`) and `SkiaSharp.QrCode` (an empty compatibility metapackage that depends on `FeatherQR.SkiaSharp` and carries no `lib/`). `tools/check_package_deps.cs` opens the packed nupkgs and asserts the exact dependency group of every target framework after every pack in CI; the expectation is a literal table in the tool, so a change to the graph is a diff someone accepts on purpose.

**The core is dependency-free where the framework carries `Span<T>`, `ArrayPool<T>` and `Unsafe`, and depends on the BCL shims where it does not.** net8.0 and net10.0 groups are empty; netstandard2.0 depends on `System.Memory` and netstandard2.1 on `System.Runtime.CompilerServices.Unsafe`. Before the split these arrived transitively through SkiaSharp, which is why removing SkiaSharp broke only the netstandard builds. "Zero dependencies" in the package description means this.

**Transitive pinning is off for the whole repository.** `CentralPackageTransitivePinningEnabled` promotes every transitive package that has a `PackageVersion` entry into the nuspec as a direct dependency, which for 1.x meant `SkiaSharp.NativeAssets.Win32` and `.macOS` beside `SkiaSharp`, and would have meant `SkiaSharp` and the native assets beside `FeatherQR.SkiaSharp` in the metapackage. The promotion changes nothing a consumer resolves (SkiaSharp brings its native assets itself) but makes the package declare a graph it does not have and the assertion above meaningless. The other half of the feature, forcing a transitive version floor on applications, has no use here: the test, benchmark, playground and sample projects are not shipped products, `NuGetAudit` reports a vulnerable resolution, and a direct `PackageReference` raises a transitive version when one ever needs raising. One setting in `Directory.Packages.props` is therefore simpler than a per-project exception that every future packable project would have to remember.

### Public API direction

Each symbology gets its own generator entry point with symbology-typed version and error-correction parameters.

**One naming rule decides every public name in both packages.** A prefix says which symbology — `QR` for Standard QR, `MicroQR`, `RmQR` — and no prefix means the type is shared by all three. A noun that literally denotes *a code* keeps the `{Sym}Code` form (`QRCodeData`, `MicroQRCodeGenerator`, `RmQRCodeDecodeInfo`); everything else, enums and ranges and strategies, takes the short prefix (`QREccLevel`, `QRSegmentation`, `QRVersionRange`). Three-letter acronyms are Pascal-cased (`Ecc`, `Eci`, `Bom`). The rule was implicit while Micro QR and rMQR were built, which is why those two already followed it; 2.0.0 applied it to the Standard QR types written first (`ECCLevel`, `QRCodeSegmentation`, `QRCodeVersionRange`) and to the shared types that had taken the `QRCode` prefix while meaning the whole family (`QRCodeDecodeStatus` became `DecodeStatus`, and in the rendering package `QRCodeRenderer` and `QRCodeImageBuilderBase<TSelf>` became `SymbolRenderer` and `SymbolImageBuilderBase<TSelf>`, the word both standards use). The defect the rule removes is that double meaning: `QRCode` cannot be Standard QR in one type name and the family in the next. `QRCodeExtensions` became `SKCanvasExtensions` under the neighbouring BCL habit of naming an extension holder after what it extends.

**The method name repeats what the class already says, so it says nothing.** `QRCodeGenerator.CreateQrCode`, `MicroQRCodeGenerator.CreateMicroQRCode` and `RmQRCodeGenerator.CreateRmQRCode` are all `Create` since 2.0.0. That also deletes rather than answers the `Qr` versus `QR` casing question those method names carried, and it is why the rule needs no clause about it.

**Options live in a per-symbology options struct, and since 2.0.0 that is the only way to configure a generator.** `QRCodeGeneratorOptions`, `MicroQRCodeGeneratorOptions` and `RmQRCodeGeneratorOptions` are `readonly record struct`s passed by `in`, so the allocation-free entry points stay allocation-free. The parameter list overloads that 1.1.1 released were frozen through 1.2.0 (exact signatures, exceptions and messages, never another parameter) and removed in 2.0.0; rMQR never had them. The rule exists because the parameter list shape had already failed on rMQR before it shipped, at 10 methods with up to 9 parameters, with one option escaping into method names: `EciMode` could not be added positionally without disturbing the existing order, so `CreateRmQRCodeWithEci` and two siblings were added instead, doubling the method count while Standard QR expressed the same concept as an ordinary parameter.

**The reshaping was possible only because of a release window.** No rMQR API had ever been in a NuGet package, so its surface could be fixed by deletion at zero compatibility cost; Standard QR and Micro QR had no such freedom and kept their released overloads. Package validation against the last published package is what enforced the difference (`EnablePackageValidation` with `PackageValidationBaselineVersion`), and the baseline was then pinned at 1.1.1 for the rest of the 1.x line rather than moving with each release, so the surface 1.2.0 added was never covered by one; it is unset on the 2.0.0 packages until 2.0.0 ships. A minor release cannot reopen that window; the 2.0.0 major is what let the deprecation cycle finish, and anything wanting the same change again waits for the next major.

**Package validation only polices the half of a change that breaks somebody, so the exported surface is also held to a listing in the repository.** Validation answers "would this break a caller who compiled against the last release", and a new public member never does: it lands unreviewed, which is the wrong default for a library whose next release is a rename. `src/FeatherQR/PublicAPI.approved.txt` and `src/FeatherQR.SkiaSharp/PublicAPI.approved.txt` record every exported type and member of the two assemblies and are regenerated by `tools/check_public_api.cs`, gated on pull requests and again at release. Changing the surface is therefore a diff someone accepts deliberately, and the 2.0.0 reshaping arrives as one reviewable file rather than as a claim in a pull request description.

**On a builder option, `null` means the option is absent and never "the default value".** A default that has a name is passed by name: `RectangleModuleShape.Default` and `RectangleFinderPatternShape.Default` for plain shapes, `SKColors.Black` and `SKColors.White` for the two colours. Through 2.0.0-preview.2 the fluent setters spelled those states as `null` as well, which bought a second spelling of a state that already had one and let `WithColors`'s optional parameters read as "leave the rest alone" while behaving as "reset the rest" — appending `.WithColors(clearColor: …)` to a chain discarded the colours an earlier call had set. 2.0.0 made the colours and both shape setters non-nullable, cut `WithColors` down to the two colours a symbol always has (both required), and added `WithCodeColor` / `WithBackgroundColor` / `WithClearColor` so one colour can be changed on its own. The nulls that survive are the ones that name an absence rather than a value: no gradient, no icon, and no clear colour of its own, which leaves the padding following the background. **`WithFinderPatternShape` was the row that had to be measured rather than reasoned about.** Omitting it is not the same code path as naming the square — the finders are drawn with the modules, and `RectangleFinderPatternShape.Default` is substituted only once the modules are styled, which is the rule that styling never reaches a finder pattern — so it read as a third state, *auto*. Rendered and compared, the two spellings differ in 0 bytes of 360,000 with plain modules, with a transparent background, and with circle modules at 0.85: same output, two draw paths, so the null was a second spelling and the fast path is an implementation detail the builder keeps for callers who never ask for a shape. The static `SymbolRenderer` and `SKCanvas.Render` surfaces keep `null` for every option, and the reason is the language rather than the rule: a C# optional parameter needs a constant default, and neither a shape instance nor black is one, so there `null` is the only spelling of "argument not supplied". Nothing renders differently either way, since the renderer already resolved each `null` to exactly those values.

**The listing is read from every target framework, which turned an assumption into a fact.** The library builds for four, nothing had ever compared them, and the claim that no exported member is framework-conditional lived only in a tool comment. It held when the gate was introduced, and a build where it stops holding now fails instead of shipping. Two renderers of the same surface exist on purpose, the reflection one behind the Playground's API page and the metadata one behind the gate, and their agreeing line for line is what keeps either from drifting unnoticed.

The type name is `{consuming generator}Options`, mechanically, so no reader has to work out which struct belongs to which generator. This follows the BCL habit of naming an options bag after its consumer (`JsonSerializerOptions` for `JsonSerializer`) and leaves `{X}DecoderOptions` free under the same rule.

Consequences worth stating here rather than three times:

- **The `options` parameter carries a default on every entry point, and could not while the parameter lists existed.** rMQR had `in RmQRCodeGeneratorOptions options = default` from the start because its parameter list versions were deleted before release; on Standard QR and Micro QR a defaulted options parameter would have made `Create(text, ecc)` ambiguous between the two sets, so callers wrote `QRCodeGeneratorOptions.Default with { ... }` explicitly until 2.0.0 removed the other set. Sizing never had the problem: `TryGetRequiredBufferSize` was always the only sizing overload, so its options parameter was defaulted from the start. The asymmetry was a consequence of the released surface rather than a preference, which is why removing that surface was enough to end it.

- **`default(T)` must be the complete default configuration**, since it is what an omitted argument sends. Any member whose documented default is not the zero value stores an offset from that default, not a `value + 1` sentinel, so that writing the default explicitly produces the same value as not writing it and the generated equality does not report two identical option sets as different. `QuietZoneSize` is the only such member today, and its correct default differs per symbology (4, 2, 2), which is also why one shared options type is not expressible.
- **Options are not shared across symbologies.** The intersection of the three option sets is one `int` with three different correct defaults: `Version` is a different type in each, Micro QR has no ECI, and rMQR's fit options mean nothing elsewhere. A shared type would carry members invalid for two thirds of its uses and reject them at run time instead of at compile time.
- **The error correction level stays a required parameter and is deliberately not an option.** It is the only input with no correct default: L and H differ by roughly 4x in capacity, and choosing between capacity and robustness is the caller's decision, not the library's. Putting it in the options struct would force `default(T)` to encode that choice silently, which contradicts the rule above. The line this draws is that the required arguments say *what symbol you want* (the text and how robust it must be) while the options say *how to encode and render it*. The image builders do default it to `M`, which is right for a "just give me a picture" entry point and wrong for the generator.
- **A version *range* exists only where versions are totally ordered.** `QRVersionRange` (1-40) and `MicroQRVersionRange` (M1-M4) subsume the single requested version, with a pinned version as the degenerate `Exactly` case; `null` and `int?` convert implicitly so an optional version needs no branch at the call site. rMQR has no range because its 32 versions have no min/max relation, and constrains fit with `RmQRFitStrategy` and `RmQRHeight` instead.

**The `string` convenience overloads went with them.** `string` converts implicitly to `ReadOnlySpan<char>`, so `Create("text", ecc)` still binds; what the overloads added was a parameter name (`plainText` rather than `textSpan`) and a second row in every IntelliSense list. They were kept while their released counterparts pinned the shape and dropped in 2.0.0 with them, which also ended the asymmetry where only Standard QR had a `string` destination overload. Every generator is now two `Create` methods, span and span-plus-destination, plus `TryGetRequiredBufferSize`.

That reasoning was recorded as holding on all four target frameworks, and it holds on three. The conversion is compiler-synthesized rather than an operator on `System.String`, and when `ReadOnlySpan<T>` arrives from the `System.Memory` package instead of the framework — the netstandard2.0 asset, which is what .NET Framework consumers bind — only C# 14 synthesizes it. Every language version through 13 reports `CS1503` there. The lesson is that "converts implicitly" is a property of the span's provenance and the consumer's compiler, not of the target framework, and that a claim about consumer compilation has to be measured from a consumer project rather than reasoned about from the library's own build, which compiles at C# 14 and therefore proves nothing. The same measurement found the larger half: `init` accessors need C# 9, so on the netstandard2.0 (default C# 7.3) and netstandard2.1 (default C# 8.0) assets the option structs were unconfigurable once the parameter lists were gone. Each of the three, and `IconData`, now carries a constructor for that audience, which is why an option settable only through an object initializer is a defect the shape tests check for.

Decoding: matrix-level entry points are symbology-explicit (matrix size alone distinguishes Micro QR 11–17 from Standard 21–177, but rectangular input needs width/height). Image-level decoding keeps Standard-QR-only scanning as the default; additional symbologies are opt-in so the existing detection hot path keeps its performance characteristics.

**A successful image decode also says where the symbol was.** Every `*DecodeInfo` carries `Corners`, a `SymbolCorners` of four `ImagePoint`s (both shared, library-built record structs): the outer corners of the module area, quiet zone excluded, in the input's *continuous* pixel coordinates — (0, 0) is the top-left corner of the top-left pixel, so the values plot directly in SkiaSharp, a canvas or System.Drawing. No shift is applied at the boundary: the finder centres every mapping is anchored on come from run boundaries with an exclusive end and are already in that convention, so a symbol drawn from pixel 48 reports 48.0 (the first implementation added half a pixel on the theory that the samplers' `(int)(x + 0.5f)` meant "integer = pixel centre"; a tenth-of-a-pixel test on the finder-anchored corners is what caught it). The corners are named in the symbol's own frame (`TopLeft` is beside the finder that defines the symbol's top-left, wherever the camera put it), which is what lets one quadrilateral report rotation and, through reversed winding, mirroring; the square decoders retry a mirrored capture by transposing the sampled matrix, so the one bit they have to carry out is whether that retry won, while rMQR's frames swap axes and its transform is already in symbol order. The value is populated only on `Success`: a matrix decode has no image, and a failed image decode located nothing a caller should draw. It is an estimate from the fitted geometry, and the stated bound follows how much each decoder infers. Standard QR (three finders plus an alignment pattern, and for the mesh path a transform re-anchored on the mesh's far lattice node) holds half a module for flat, rotated, mirrored and keystoned captures at the tilts the corner tests run (12 % on versions 2 and 5, 6 to 8 % on 7 and 10, 5 to 6 % from version 14 up; the 8 px per module test scene decodes further on most versions, to 15 to 17 % on 2 and 5 and 10 % on 7 and 30, and holds the bound there too) — **and at 8 px per module or more**. Below that density the bound belongs in pixels, not modules: the bottom-right corner is anchored on the alignment pattern, whose centre the finder resolves to roughly a pixel at any module size, so the error is near-constant in pixels (measured on version 2 over every rotation: 4.09 px at 6 px per module, 3.63 at 8, 3.94 at 12) while the module it is divided by shrinks — 0.68 module at 6 px per module against 0.33 at 12. A second loosening is structural rather than a matter of scale: whenever the bottom-right alignment pattern is not located, `BuildGridTransform` falls back to the finders-only parallelogram quad that version 1 always gets, and error correction still returns `Success`, so a version-2-and-up symbol with one damaged module over that pattern reports an ordinary result with that corner up to about a module and a half out. The public contract states both, because nothing in `QRCodeDecodeInfo` tells a caller which fit ran. Micro QR and rMQR fit from a single finder and hold half a module flat and at right angles (rMQR also at the one oblique angle tested): an oblique Micro QR rotation is reported at whichever 1° axis angle first decodes, and the finder sweep's run-length score is flat for ±3 to 4° around the truth, so the winner is routinely 1 to 2° off and the far corners measure 0.2 to 0.9 module at any pixel scale; a Micro QR keystone through the same search measures 0.55 to 0.76 module at 5 to 8 % and 1.03 mirrored at 8 %; and rMQR's bounded perspective search under-recovers the column-axis lean on short symbols, 0.9 module at 2 % and 1.2 to 1.25 at 3 to 4 % on R11x59 at one of the two far corners (which one depends on version and tilt), while R17x139 and left/right-shrunk keystones stay under 0.65. The contract says "about a module" for those and "a module and a half" for an rMQR symbol from 2 % up (measured at 2 %: nine versions over a module, worst R7x99 at 1.22 and R15x99 at 1.19, so the threshold is 2 % and it is not confined to short symbols); tightening them means a post-decode frame refit, listed as a follow-up in the plan. `System.Numerics.Vector2` was not used because on netstandard2.0 it would add a package dependency to a package that advertises none. No reference library returns this for Standard QR, which is why it was worth a public type.

Image builders: one builder per symbology, all deriving from `SymbolImageBuilderBase<TSelf>` (self-referential generic, so fluent chains keep the concrete type). The base carries every shared option and the complete raster/SVG output surface; a symbology builder adds only its typed options (ECC/version) and connects its data model through three `private protected` hooks. Two guards keep the surfaces from drifting: the base class makes output-method omissions structurally impossible, and `QrImageBuilderApiParityTest` (reflection over the public surfaces with a documented allowed-difference list) catches asymmetry in what cannot be shared, the symbology-typed static helpers. The rMQR builder extends the same base and the same parity test.

Capacity pricing overflow: Byte mode costs `8 × length` bits, so a data length past `int.MaxValue / 8` wraps negative and reads as a fit. All three selectors price in `long` — including the UTF-8 BOM's `+ 3`, which wraps on its own near `int.MaxValue`. Widening rather than rejecting the length up front is the deliberate choice: a length fast-path placed ahead of the remaining checks answers "does not fit" for what is actually an argument error, and one placed ahead of the Micro QR version check also handed an unvalidated version to the table-indexing error builder. Reachable only with a quarter-gigabyte input, so `CapacityOverflowGuardTest` drives the selectors directly instead of allocating one.

Sizing: every generator exposes exactly one sizing method, `TryGetRequiredBufferSize`, with one contract across all three symbologies — `false` means the content does not fit, and argument errors throw. Standard QR and Micro QR carried an `[Obsolete]` throwing `GetRequiredBufferSize` through 1.2.0, kept only because v1.1.1 released it, and lost it in 2.0.0. `SizingSurfaceTest` asserts the absence rather than assuming it, because a throwing convenience is the kind of thing someone re-adds in good faith. The reasoning, including why this is a `Try` overload rather than a dedicated exception type and why undefined enum values are not folded into `false`, is recorded once in [rmqr-encoder.md](rmqr-encoder.md); the other two symbologies follow it rather than restating it.

Exact API names and shapes are finalized per-symbology at implementation time, spec-first, following the API-driven development principle in [DESIGN.md](../DESIGN.md).

### Data model direction

`QRCodeData` stays Standard-QR-only. New symbologies get their own data types, with rectangular dimensions (width ≠ height) decided once when the first new type is introduced.

Serialization: the `QRR` format is frozen as-is for Standard QR (header + 1-byte size, sizes 21–177, square). New symbologies use a new serialization header carrying symbol type, width, and height. Old readers reject new-format streams cleanly (the existing header/size validation already guarantees this).

**A value the library hands back is a `readonly record struct` with an internal constructor and get-only properties.** `QRCodeCalculatedSize`, `MicroQRCodeCalculatedSize`, `RmQRCodeCalculatedSize` and the three `*DecodeInfo` types all follow it since 2.0.0; Standard QR's sizing result had a public constructor, `init` setters and an `IsValid` property, the other two were plain structs, and the drift was invisible until someone read all three files side by side. The rule is what the type is *for*: it is an `out` parameter of a `Try` method, so there is no half-built instance to hand back in, `init` would let a caller edit an answer the library computed, and `IsValid` duplicated the `bool` the `Try` already returned. Only positional records deconstruct, so declaring these without positional parameters drops deconstruction and keeps everything else — `ToString`, `==` and `IEquatable<T>` — which is what a caller logging a size or comparing two decode results actually uses. `TypeShapeTest` asserts the shape rather than trusting the next type to copy it.

**Being library-built is not a reason to be opaque, and that took two attempts.** The first cut demoted these to plain structs, which also threw away the printer and non-boxing equality: `size.ToString()` became the type name and `Equals` started boxing both operands. What had to go was the public constructor and the `init` setters; the record was never the problem. The same mistake landed on `GradientOptions` in the same change, where dropping the record silently removed `with`. One rule came out of it: when a type's shape is wrong, name the member that is wrong and remove that, rather than reaching for the enclosing kind.

**The three decode results report the same members under the same names**, with one documented exception: rMQR has no `MaskPattern`, because ISO/IEC 23941 defines a single data mask. Same for sizing, where rMQR is rectangular (`Width`/`Height`) and the square symbologies report one `Size`.

**An option object a caller builds is immutable once built, and stays varyable with `with`.** The generator options are `readonly record struct`s with `init` members; `IconData` is a `sealed record class` with `init`-only members, and `GradientOptions` is a `sealed record class` that copies the arrays it is given and reads them back as `ReadOnlySpan<T>`. They vary with `with`, which is the point: changing one field of an instance a caller did not construct — a preset from configuration, an `IconData` from a factory method — otherwise means retyping every other field and silently taking the defaults for the ones forgotten.

**A member is `init` when it carries no cross-member invariant, and set through a method or the constructor when it does.** `with` assigns one member at a time, so a pair that must agree cannot be exposed that way: `GradientOptions.Colors` and `ColorPositions` have to be the same length, and making them `init` would let a caller build a gradient whose stops no longer match its colours and discover it at draw time. `Direction` has no such pairing and stays `init`; the pair is set together through the constructor, which refuses the mismatch on the spot. `IconData` needs no such carve-out because none of its members validate against another at construction — its sizing rules are checked when the icon is drawn, so every member can be `init`. The rule is what makes the two types differ, not an oversight in either. `GradientOptions` is where this stopped being theoretical: holding a public `SKColor[]` through an `init` property, its generated equality compared the arrays by reference, so two identical gradients were unequal, and `GradientOptions.Default` — one shared instance — could be repainted for the whole process through the array it exposed. **An immutable type has to be rebuildable from what it hands back.** `GradientOptions` first exposed spans and accepted arrays, with "no stops" reading as an empty span and writing as `null`, so recolouring an existing gradient cost a `ToArray()` and a ternary — and a caller who omitted the ternary silently dropped the stops. The constructor takes spans now, empty meaning evenly distributed on both sides, and the round trip is one expression. The rule generalises: when a value type's getter and its constructor disagree about representation, the migration guide is where the disagreement shows up as an unreadable line, and the guide is the wrong place to fix it.

Equality is written by hand over the elements now, and the array is private, which is also what makes the record's shallow copy safe: `Default with { Direction = … }` shares the colours with `Default`, and no member of either instance hands the array out. The guarantee documented is "immutable through the API" rather than "immutable", because `MemoryMarshal` and reflection both reach past it — not a caveat worth putting in front of callers, but the qualifier keeps a later change from treating the array as unreachable. Dropping the record was tried first and rejected — it took `with` away while the three generator options kept it, and the defect was the *public array*, not the record. `IconData` was demoted the same way in the same change and restored for the same reason.

**Styling reaches the data modules, never the finder patterns.** `WithModuleShape(shape, sizePercent)` and its renderer parameters style the data; the finder patterns are drawn as one continuous concentric pattern whatever is asked for, and `WithFinderPatternShape` (on all three builders) is the only way to change how they look. The split is not aesthetic, it is how the two kinds of module are read: a data module is sampled at the centre of its cell, so gaps around it cost nothing, while a finder is located by scanning for its 1:1:3:1:1 run of dark and light, which a gap of one fiftieth of a module already destroys — the dark three-module centre becomes three runs and the ratio is nowhere in the image. Measured: at 98 % module size the symbol was found by neither this library nor ZXing, on every symbology, so what the old behaviour produced was a non-conformant symbol rather than a styled one (ISO/IEC 15415 grades fixed-pattern damage separately from data for the same reason). Alignment patterns need no such protection and get none: they are found from a predicted position by their single dark centre module, and shrinking them to 75 % still decodes at version 40. The full-size square path is left in the merged-run renderer, where the finder is already solid, so the fast path is untouched and only the per-module path pays anything — and it pays less, three rectangles per finder instead of thirty-three module draws.

**Modules stay square at every canvas aspect ratio the builder accepts, so `WithSize(w, h)` fits rather than stretches.** That is the invariant, and it is deliberately narrower than "every canvas produces a readable symbol": what a reader needs is square modules *and* enough pixels per module, and `WithSize` has no lower bound on the second. A canvas can starve the short side without being small (4000x30 is 0.91 px/module and nothing reads it), so the fit removes one failure mode rather than all of them. The symbol is drawn at one uniform module scale, centered, whatever aspect ratio the caller asks for; leftover canvas is padded with `clearColor` when one is set and with the background colour otherwise. Both halves are corrections of the same defect on the square symbologies (rMQR was built this way, except that its explicit-canvas pad was transparent). The stretch dates to the 2019 renderer, which divided the area by columns and rows independently, and to a public API that took width and height separately from its first release; nothing chose it, and nothing tested it, so it survived into 2.0.0 behind a `preserveAspectRatio` flag whose comment said only that the square symbologies "keep the historical fill behavior". What it produced was undetectable rather than merely ugly: module centres stayed correct, so the data was intact and no call threw, while the finder's 1:1:3:1:1 run only survives on one axis once the cells are rectangular. Sweeping several payloads, four stylings and both orientations through this library and ZXing.Net, failures appear from about 1.25:1 and neither reads anything past about 1.8:1; where a given symbol lands in between moves with the payload, with the styling and with which axis is squeezed, and the two decoders disagree by direction (on wide renders this library reads many ZXing does not; on tall ones ZXing reads many this library does not, though that half depends on ZXing being run with AutoRotate). There is no threshold worth quoting, which is the point — `WithSize(900, 450)` returned an image neither of them reads (zxing-cpp, outside that sweep, reads the migration guide's example, though not every payload), and nothing said so. The pad default follows from the same standard: transparent is the wrong thing to hand back by default, because it becomes black bands the moment the image is encoded as JPEG and it costs the opaque-surface optimization; transparent surroundings around an opaque symbol stay available by naming `clearColor`. The pad is painted around the content rather than under it, so a translucent background is not blended twice.

**The low-level renderer fits its area too, so the library has one geometry rule (2026-09-11).** `SymbolRenderer.Render(canvas, area, …)` and the `SKCanvas.Render` extensions draw Standard QR and Micro QR at one uniform module scale centered in the area, with the background over the whole area, which is what rMQR's overload always did. The public `GetFinderPatternRect` and `GetIconRects` fit the same way, because they answer for the area the caller passed to `Render` and would otherwise point beside what was drawn. For a day after the builders stopped stretching, the renderer kept the fill on purpose, as the only way left to pre-distort a symbol for an output device whose dots are not square, and the plan was to give the builders an axis-aware module size first and only then make the renderer fit. Checking that plan found its premise false. Pre-distortion never needed a stretched area: a non-uniform canvas scale over a square area gives the old fill's pixels exactly for plain modules and finders in a solid colour (0 differing pixels across four aspect ratios; styled output, meaning shaped modules or finders, gradients and icons, is drawn in the square and stretched with it, which can differ from what the old fill drew), and a square area passes through the fit unchanged, so the renderer fits and the device case is served by the canvas transform, where a caller who owns the canvas already says such things. The builder-level `WithModulePixelSize(x, y)` waits for a concrete request: the device use case was named in review to justify the fill and has no report behind it, and it would have to be built as a transform over square cells: the renderer fits any non-square area it is handed to a square, and a path that skipped the fit would still get styled modules wrong, since `CircleModuleShape` sizes its dot from the shorter side of the cell and would print squashed, and the rounded shapes take their corner radius from that side and would print uneven corners. The fit is taken from the shorter side rather than through a module scale, and an area already square to within float rounding comes back exactly as given, so a square area draws what it drew before and fitting twice equals fitting once; the renderer relies on that when it hands an already-fitted area to the helpers. The rounding slack is not optional: `SKRect.Create(x, y, s, s)` stores right and bottom as rounded sums, so a square at fractional coordinates is often a float step from square, and shrinking it by that step moved module edges by a pixel. Two float steps per axis is the floor, not a margin: a square whose four edges are each scaled, which is what a canvas scale produces, comes back two steps from square, measured over three million of them against `SKRect.Create`, centre-and-half and `SKMatrix.MapRect` constructions. The cost of that floor is that far from the origin, where a step is a large share of the area, a rectangle that is not square passes as one: at 1e9 a step is 64, so a 400x600 area is stored as 384x576, one and a half steps from square, and is drawn square. Nothing renders correctly there in any case, because the same step quantises every module edge, and no slack can separate the two: the rectangle is closer to square, in steps, than a real scaled square is. The two limits are far apart, measured on a 400 px symbol: a square area stops decoding at a coordinate of 1.68e7 (2^24), where a step reaches 2 and the module edges quantise, while the slack does not accept a 1.5:1 area until 4.38e8 (2^28.7), twenty-six times further out. Inside the range that still decodes, the widest stretch the slack can accept is about 1 % (1.011:1 at a coordinate of 1e7), against the 1.25:1 where reading starts to fail, so the slack cannot cost a read. The precision is lost in the caller's `SKRect` before the renderer sees it, so no signature taking one can recover it; a caller working at such coordinates keeps the area near the origin and places it with the canvas transform, which is what the rasteriser wants anyway. An inverted area (a negative width or height) is refused with `ArgumentException` in all three symbologies, and so is a non-finite one: an inverted rect reads two ways, a mirror or the same bounds written backwards, and for an asymmetric symbol those are different pictures, so neither is guessed. A mirrored symbol is asked for with a canvas scale of -1 about the area, the same principle as pre-distortion, and the decoder reads mirrored captures, so strict output and tolerant input stay the pair. A zero-size area draws nothing rather than throwing, because a canvas before layout or a collapsed panel produces one routinely; the test is the fitted symbol, so anything sized in pixels rather than in cells (an icon border, a caption, a caller-written shape) stops there too, while invalid icon settings are still refused, since a collapsed panel must not hide a mistake until it opens. An area whose fitted symbol has no size keeps its background, since the area is the caller's and only the symbol is missing; an aspect ratio past about 2^25 reaches that state without being zero, because centring the symbol puts its offset where its shorter side rounds away (rMQR's rectangle survives about three powers of two longer than the square symbologies'). The canvas extensions check every argument before they clear the canvas, so a refused call leaves it as it was, which means the gradient direction is checked up front as well, not left to the draw call that consumes it. What still differs from the builders is rounding: they floor the centering offset to whole pixels because they own the canvas, while the renderer uses the fit as computed because its area may sit under the caller's transform, so an odd leftover can shift edges by half a pixel. The decode side keeps its non-square tolerance: symbols arrive from thermal printers, laser markers and perspective, so an encoder that never produces non-square modules and a decoder that accepts them is the pair that makes sense. The tolerance has a measured edge, the same for all three symbologies (plain modules 8 px on the short side, three payloads per symbology, every right-angle rotation, 2026-09-12): up to about 1.38:1 every rotation decodes; from about 1.4:1 to about 1.65:1 modules wider than tall decode and modules taller than wide mostly do not, the exact edge depending on the payload (Standard QR still reads two of three test payloads taller than wide at 1.40:1, none at 1.41:1); from 1.70:1 nothing decodes. With the builders and the renderer fitting every area, a canvas scale is the only way left to make such a symbol, so the decoder tests draw theirs that way and measure the finder's centre stone on both axes to prove the stretch is in the pixels; the tests they replaced had been drawing square modules since the canvas fit, and nothing noticed.

**A public class with no designed extension point is sealed:** the three data types, the three image builders, `IconData` and `GradientOptions`. The extension points are the shape hierarchies (`ModuleShape`, `FinderPatternShape`, `IconShape`), and `SymbolImageBuilderBase<TSelf>`, whose `private protected` constructor keeps derivation inside the rendering package.

## Why

### Why three packages under a new name

Issue #370 named the two strengths of the 1.x library, SkiaSharp integration and speed with low memory, and the contradiction between them: anyone who wanted only the QR module matrices still paid for SkiaSharp. The cost was never the managed assembly (95 KB trimmed to QR encode only); it is `libSkiaSharp`, 11.9 MB per RID, untrimmable, deployed whether or not a Skia call survives, and the part that needs CVE tracking. A dependency graph is fixed only by a package boundary, so the 2.0.0 major split the one package into a dependency-free core and a rendering package (the core split, 2026-09-04 to 2026-09-06).

**The core is not `SkiaSharp.QrCode.Core`.** A dependency-free package must not carry the name of the dependency it is free of; the name would lie to exactly the audience the split is for, and it fails at the second non-Skia renderer (`SkiaSharp.QrCode.ImageSharp` is nonsense). The `SkiaSharp.*` prefix is reserved on nuget.org but public, so the ID was pushable; it was rejected on meaning, not mechanics. The brand became `FeatherQR`: "Feather" is the established .NET word for lightweight (`FeatherHttp`, `Feather.Blazor`, `DotFeather`), lightweight is the title of the issue, and the compound was free on nuget.org, npm, crates.io, PyPI and GitHub. Every speed word considered instead was a benchmark claim, a live product, a reduced-feature connotation, a language, a fictional symbology next to Micro QR, or a .NET-only term. What the name is allowed to mean is defined under "Package architecture" so it never has to be defended against a byte count.

**`SkiaSharp.QrCode` survives as an empty metapackage because NuGet has no redirect.** The three mechanisms that exist are keeping an ID, deprecating it with an alternate (one-way, for retiring), and a metapackage. Only the last keeps an existing `<PackageReference Include="SkiaSharp.QrCode" />` restoring after the upgrade, which is the whole point behind four million downloads. New documentation leads with `FeatherQR.SkiaSharp`; the metapackage is the compatibility door, not the front door, and it stays for as long as 1.x packages are listed.

**One namespace per package, no type forwarding.** `FeatherQR` and `FeatherQR.SkiaSharp`; the former `SkiaSharp.QrCode.Image` sub-namespace is folded into the rendering namespace because the major changes every `using` line anyway. Type forwarding was not used: the same major renames types, so a forward would preserve nothing anyone can compile against.

**`TryDecode(SKBitmap)` is a C# 14 extension member with a named fallback.** A static method cannot be added to a type from another assembly, and every renderer package has the same need. Extension blocks solve it once: `QRCodeImageDecoder` (and the Micro QR and rMQR twins) declares `extension(QRCodeDecoder)` with the bitmap overloads, the compiler emits them as ordinary public statics on the enclosing class, and so a C# 14 consumer writes `QRCodeDecoder.TryDecode(bitmap, ...)` while a C# 12 or 13 consumer (net8.0's default) writes `QRCodeImageDecoder.TryDecode(bitmap, ...)`. One source, no `#if`; the documentation shows the enclosing-class form first because most consumers will see only that form for years, and the migration guide says why the 1.x spelling can stop compiling on net8.0 so it is not reported as a missing overload.

**Lockstep versions, one tag, one release run.** `Directory.Build.props` keeps its single `<Version>`; the `ProjectReference` from the rendering package to the core becomes a package dependency at that version on pack; the release workflow's push glob already covered several packages. Prerelease versions are a manual edit because `bump_version.cs` produces `X.Y.Z` only.

**Order: split first, renames second, previews in between.** The split is structural and touches every file; the 2.0.0 type renames are textual and touch every consumer. Done together they would have produced a diff nobody could review. The split shipped as `2.0.0-preview.1` to claim the three IDs and exercise the pipeline, the repository rename shipped as `2.0.0-preview.2` to prove Trusted Publishing under the new name, and the type renames follow as their own plan before `2.0.0`.

**The repository followed the brand, and the Playground URL was handled explicitly.** GitHub redirects the web URL and every `git` operation from the old name indefinitely as long as the old name is never reused; GitHub Pages project sites are the documented exception, and the old Playground URL is printed in the README of every 1.x package on nuget.org, which cannot be edited. A path with no project site behind it falls through to the user site, so `SkiaSharp.QrCode/index.html` (and `api/index.html`) on `guitarrapc/guitarrapc.github.io` serve the old URLs and forward, by script so that the query and the hash (where shared Playground links keep their settings) survive, with a meta refresh as the no-script fallback. Creating a repository under the old name to host the stub would have broken the repository redirect and was ruled out. The nuget.org Trusted Publishing policy is bound to owner and repository name and was updated in the same window.

### Why separate entry points instead of extending `Create`

The existing parameters do not generalize:

| Parameter | Standard QR | Micro QR | rMQR |
|---|---|---|---|
| Version | `int` 1–40 | M1–M4 | R7x43–R17x139 (32 rectangular sizes) |
| ECC level | L/M/Q/H | M1: detection only; M2–M3: L/M; M4: L/M/Q | M/H only |
| Auto-selection | Smallest version | Smallest version, mode legality varies per version | Fit strategy is two-dimensional (width-first vs height-first) |

Overloading one method family with union-typed parameters would make illegal combinations representable and push validation to runtime. Separate entry points make each symbology's constraints visible in the type system.

### Why sibling namespaces instead of a polymorphic abstraction

The Standard QR pipeline is heavily performance-tuned (zero-allocation steady state, SIMD kernels, stackalloc buffers, aggressive inlining). A shared abstraction over the pipeline stages (virtual dispatch, interface indirection, or generic strategy types) would put abstraction cost on the hot path and couple all symbologies to one pipeline shape, even though their stages genuinely differ (e.g. rMQR has no mask selection, Micro QR has no interleaving for most versions, format information differs in size, location, and BCH code).

Sibling namespaces bound the blast radius instead: a Micro QR change cannot touch Standard QR code paths. The regression guard is structural (namespace dependency rule) plus empirical (Standard QR benchmarks must stay flat through every phase).

### Why `QRCodeData` is not generalized

`QRCodeData` is a shipped public type whose contract is square, 21–177 modules, versions 1–40, with a serialization format that encodes exactly that. Generalizing it would either break the serialization contract or turn every member into a symbology-conditional. Sibling data types keep the shipped contract byte-for-byte stable and let rectangular geometry be designed without compatibility constraints.

### Why Kanji mode is read but never written

Kanji is asymmetric on purpose: all three decoders read it, no generator emits it.

Reading it is an interoperability obligation. Japanese-market encoders do emit Kanji mode, and a
decoder that rejects those symbols cannot read them at all, which is a hole no caller can work
around. Writing it is a different decision: UTF-8 Byte mode already carries Japanese text, and
emitting Kanji would change the default output of shipped generators. Decoding changes no output,
so it ships on its own.

The consequence is a deliberate round-trip asymmetry: `Decode(Encode(x)) == x` holds, but
`Encode(Decode(y))` does not reproduce a Kanji symbol `y`. The capacity tables therefore keep the
Kanji column for the decoder's count-indicator widths, not as a commitment to encode.

**The mapping is JIS X 0208, not CP932.** The two disagree on seven Shift_JIS cells (0x815F,
0x8160, 0x8161, 0x817C, 0x8191, 0x8192, 0x81CA: reverse solidus, wave dash, double vertical line,
minus sign, and the cent / pound / not signs), and, within the Kanji-mode range, CP932
additionally assigns 83 characters the standard does not, all of them NEC row 13 (0x8740-0x879C:
circled digits, roman numerals, unit ligatures). Choosing CP932 would have
mangled exactly the characters Japanese payloads use in URLs and price strings. The shared
`ShiftJisKanjiTable` holds the 6,879-cell JIS X 0208 repertoire and nothing else; cells outside it
are reported as `DecodeStatus.UnmappedCharacter` rather than replaced, so a corrupt symbol never
becomes a plausible wrong answer and a caller can tell "a CP932 reader would read this" from the
structural `UnsupportedContent` cases (FNC1, Structured Append, unmapped ECI). The
table costs 16 KB of RVA data, shared by all three symbologies, with no allocation and no static
constructor.

**The table is derived from a measurement and gated by arithmetic, not transcribed.** Its values
come from a sweep of every structurally valid Kanji-mode cell (8,023 of them, encoded by qrtool as
raw Shift_JIS and read back by zxing-cpp), and the generator refuses to emit unless that swept data
reproduces JIS X 0208's published repertoire size and its delta against CP932 is exactly the
documented divergence set. Reproducing **6,879** assigned cells independently (524 non-kanji +
6,355 kanji) is what makes "this really is JIS X 0208" a measurement rather than an assumption.
Because every other table test constrains only *which* cells are assigned and would pass a table
whose readings were permuted, a golden digest over all 8,192 entries pins the values themselves;
regenerating the table is expected to change it, in the same reviewed commit.

Two failure causes are kept apart on the error path: a structurally impossible byte pair is
`InvalidBitstream`, a well-formed but unassigned cell is `UnmappedCharacter`. The distinguishing
arithmetic sits on the error path only, so the happy path stays a single indexed load.

Still unsupported and still reported as `UnsupportedContent`: ECI 20 (Shift_JIS) byte-mode
segments, which need the wider CP932 single-byte plus double-byte range, and (Standard QR) FNC1
and Structured Append.

### Allocation contract

The span-destination overloads are documented as allocating nothing **per call**, not as
never touching the heap. Every symbology lazily builds immutable lookup tables on first use
and caches them for the process: per-version placement and extraction layouts, and — on
ARM64, where the syndrome kernel reads its data terms out of a table rather than computing
them — a 24 KB alpha-step table shared by all three symbologies. They are built once, keyed
by version, published with a release store, and bounded (about 100 KB if every rMQR version
were exercised). A benchmark that measures allocation must warm up first, or it attributes
that one-time build to the call that happened to trigger it.

### SIMD tier inventory

Shared primitives that already have both an x64 and an ARM64/Vector128 tier, and must be
treated as controls rather than reimplemented when a new symbology or kernel arrives:
`TextAnalyzer`, `EccBinaryEncoder`, `EccBinaryDecoder` (syndrome pass), `ModuleBitPacker`,
`LuminanceConverter`, `LuminanceInverter`, and finder/alignment row-mask construction.
Architecture-neutral work already benefits every target: cached per-version layouts, pair
stores and index scatter, table-driven auto-fit, the portable extraction walk, the safe
finder stride with full-sweep retry, sub-finder guards, and Otsu reuse.

The ARM64 optimization queue is closed. Four components were measured and deliberately left
below it, with reasons: Otsu histogramming (serial histogram updates, already near its
measured per-pixel floor), sub-finder and perspective search (branchy, data-dependent and
failure-path dominated), rendering and PNG encode (Skia/native-code dominated), and the
1.3-8.3 ns version selector. Reopen ARM work only with a new profile naming a different
mechanism.

## Scope decisions

| Decision | Choice | Revisit when |
|---|---|---|
| Package topology | `FeatherQR` (core) + `FeatherQR.SkiaSharp` (renderer) + `SkiaSharp.QrCode` (empty metapackage); one core for all three symbologies, split at the leaf | Never for the core split itself. The metapackage is retired only after the last 1.x listing is gone from nuget.org |
| Per-symbology core packages | Rejected: saves untrimmed consumers 100 to 130 KB of 384 KB, costs a four-package core with a public surface for the shared kernels; trimmed consumers already get one symbology (95 KB for QR encode only) | Trimming stops being precise, which only a unified entry point could cause, and that is never added |
| Luminance conversion API | Internal (`LuminanceConverter.Convert` + `PixelLayout`), reached by the first-party renderer through `InternalsVisibleTo`; third parties decode through `TryDecodeImage` with their own luminance | A concrete request for a non-Skia first-class decode adapter; promotion is a visibility change, the adapter shape is already single-entry |
| `InternalsVisibleTo` from the core to `FeatherQR.SkiaSharp` | Permanent for first-party packages; every use enumerated under "Package seam" with a replacement or a reason | A listed use gains a public replacement (the enumeration shrinks); the grant itself stays |
| Pure-BCL SVG writer and 1-bit PNG writer in the core | Not built. They belong in the core (no Skia needed to emit either) and would let a `FeatherQR`-only consumer produce an image file | A request for image output without SkiaSharp; `GetModuleRectangles` already gives the geometry an SVG writer needs |
| Additional renderer packages (ImageSharp, System.Drawing, ...) | None. The split makes them possible; a renderer draws from `GetModuleRectangles` and decodes through `TryDecodeImage` | A request with a concrete consumer |
| The announced removals (`GetRequiredBufferSize`, `Compression`, parameter-list generator overloads) | Done in 2.0.0-preview.3. Every generator now takes only `in {Sym}CodeGeneratorOptions`, defaulted | Never; a throwing sizing method is asserted absent |
| 2.0.0 type renames (the `QR` casing rule, `QREccLevel` to `QREccLevel` and friends) and the `string` convenience overloads | Out of the split and out of the removals; their own plan, same major, before `2.0.0` final | That plan |
| Pages fallback stub on the user site | Kept for as long as 1.x packages are listed on nuget.org, since their READMEs link the old Playground URL | Never while a 1.x listing exists |
| Kanji mode (all symbologies) | Decode only, JIS X 0208 mapping; encoders keep emitting UTF-8 Byte mode (with ECI where the symbology supports it) | Encoding: a policy change backed by concrete demand, since it alters shipped generator output |
| ECI 20 (Shift_JIS) byte segments | Unsupported; reported as `UnsupportedContent` (structural, unlike the per-character `UnmappedCharacter`) | Demand for symbols that pair ECI 20 with Byte mode; needs the full CP932 range, roughly twice the Kanji table |
| Image detection default | Standard QR only (`QRCodeDecoder`); Micro QR and rMQR scanning are their own explicitly-typed entries (`MicroQRCodeDecoder`, `RmQRCodeDecoder`); the Playground tries the three in that order | - |
| Shared detection primitives (Otsu, run-ratio scan) | Lifted to `Internals.ImageDecoders` (Phase 4b, second consumer appeared) | - |
| `QRCodeData` | Frozen for Standard QR | Never (compatibility contract) |
| Interoperability runs against external encoders/decoders | Manual, not a CI job. `tools/QRInteropFixtures` spot-checks (`spot-check-rmqr`, `spot-check-microqr`) are run by hand before a release; pull-request CI stays self-contained and consumes the committed fixture corpus instead | A regression the committed corpus cannot catch, or an external oracle that installs cleanly enough for scheduled CI under the pinning policy in [qrcode-test-fixtures.md](qrcode-test-fixtures.md) |
| Physical scanner acceptance | Not automated, and deliberately never a conformance gate: a phone scanner disagreeing proves an interoperability problem, never a specification violation. Run ad hoc against a representative print/screen set before a symbology's first release | A field report that the committed corpus and the image-degradation tests both pass but real scanners fail |

## Lessons learned

- **A claim about *consumer* compilation cannot be checked from the library's own build.** The library compiles at C# 14, so it proves nothing about what a consumer at the SDK-default language version can write; "`string` converts implicitly on all four target frameworks" was recorded as fact and is false for the netstandard2.0 asset. Checking it needs a consumer project per target framework at the default language version, and preferably one that also runs. The same measurement is what found that `init`-only options were unconfigurable there once the parameter lists were gone (see "Public API direction" above).
- **A differential test dies with the thing it compares against.** Three test classes proved the options overloads equalled the released parameter lists; deleting the parameter lists would have left them comparing a call to itself. The output of every configuration was captured from the released overloads immediately before the removal and frozen as expected values (version, matrix size, SHA-256 of the serialized matrix and of the destination buffer), which is the stronger guarantee: it now catches an encoder change, not just a disagreement between two spellings. The sizing sweeps went the other way and were re-pointed at the encode itself — a buffer sized by `TryGetRequiredBufferSize` has to be the buffer `Create*` fills — which is the invariant a caller actually depends on. Deciding this *before* deleting is what made it possible; after the deletion the values are unrecoverable. The same sweep left one behind: `ArgumentErrorPrecedenceTest` compared the options path against the parameter list path, and the Phase 1 removal sweep rewrote the removed spelling into the surviving one instead of deleting the test, so it sat on this branch comparing a call to a textually identical copy of itself until the pre-PR review; it reached no tag and no released package. Converting the three classes that were noticed did not make the rule hold; only re-reading every test that named a removed member did.
- **The two removed sizing overloads disagreed with each other about exception types, and that was frozen for two releases.** Measured, not read off the docs, which had drifted: Standard QR reported a content overflow as `InvalidOperationException` while Micro QR reported the same condition as `ArgumentException`, and Standard QR reported an undefined `QREccLevel` as `ArgumentException` where Micro QR and rMQR use `ArgumentOutOfRangeException`. Both shipped in v1.1.1, so changing either was exactly the break the deprecation window existed to avoid. The lesson outlives them: an exception tag is the one part of a public API with no compiler behind it, which is why it drifted, and why a test rather than proofreading was the fix.
- **`required` members put `[Obsolete]` on every constructor that is not annotated `[SetsRequiredMembers]`**, and a metadata-level API listing renders that as if it were a deprecation. `IconData` read as carrying an announced removal in `PublicAPI.approved.txt` and does not; the marker is how the compiler stops a pre-C#-11 consumer from bypassing the required-member check. Read a listing entry against the source before acting on it.
- **A blanket identifier rewrite reaches third-party API with the same spelling.** `ECCLevel` → `QREccLevel` renamed `QRCoder.QRCodeGenerator.ECCLevel` in the comparator benchmarks too; only the compiler caught it. Any repository-wide rename of a common name has to be read back against the build, and a comparator benchmark is where the collision lives.
- **PowerShell's `-ne` is case-insensitive**, so `if ($new -ne $old) { write }` silently skips a case-only rename — `Internals.RmQr` → `Internals.RmQR` wrote nothing on the first pass, and only the compiler's "type does not exist" said so. Case-only renames need `-cne`, and on a case-insensitive filesystem the directory needs two `git mv` hops.
- **A removal is a rename in disguise, and the compiler only finds half of it.** Deleting the parameter list overloads broke 119 call sites the compiler named, and one more it could not: `requestedVersion: -1` meant "automatic", while `QRVersionRange` rejects `-1` on purpose, so the mechanical rewrite produced code that compiled and threw at run time. The test suite caught it; a consumer's would too, which is why the migration guide leads with that trap rather than with the argument-to-property table.
- **A blanket rename sweep reaches this repository's own released package, not just third-party API.** `samples/Dotfiles/FinderPatternAlwaysBlack.cs` pins `#:package SkiaSharp.QrCode@1.0.0` as a bug repro, and the Phase 2 sweep rewrote its calls to the unreleased 2.0.0 names, so a file that built on `main` no longer compiled against the package it names. It is the QRCoder lesson one directory over, and the reason that file now carries a comment telling the next sweep to skip it. Nothing in CI builds `samples/Dotfiles`, so only a hand-run found it.
- **A case-only rename needs a case-sensitive oracle, and on Windows neither the filesystem nor `git status` is one.** Twenty-nine spec-map links, plus one mention in prose, pointed at `Internals/StandardQr/` long after that folder became `StandardQR` — stale for three releases, because a link checker that resolves against the disk reports every one of them as fine on a case-insensitive filesystem. The rename that prompted the sweep, `Internals/RmQr` to `Internals/RmQR`, had stranded only one prose mention of its own. Resolving each link against `git ls-files` is what found the rest, and re-reading `git diff` before committing is what proved the fix was really staged.

- ZXing.Net (the in-CI cross-validation oracle for Standard QR) cannot decode Micro QR or rMQR, so in-CI cross-verification is unavailable for the new symbologies. Committed external fixtures are the primary conformance oracle instead, see [qrcode-test-fixtures.md](qrcode-test-fixtures.md).
- **The Kanji divergence set is seven cells, not the six usually quoted.** 0x815F (reverse solidus U+005C against fullwidth U+FF3C) is not on the commonly circulated list and does diverge, while 0x815C, which is on it, agrees (both U+2015). Building the override list from memory would have shipped two wrong cells; the sweep found both at once.
- **CP932 does not report unassigned cells as unmapped.** .NET returns U+30FB for them, so a naive "did it decode?" comparison counts 1,061 phantom assignments on top of the 83 real NEC row 13 characters. Any comparison against CP932 has to know that, and it is why the generator gates on published totals rather than on a decode-succeeded filter.
- NEC row 13 (0x8740-0x879C: circled digits, roman numerals, unit ligatures) resolved cleanly against the same arithmetic: CP932 assigns 83 of its 92 structurally valid cells, zxing-cpp assigns none, and excluding them is exactly what makes the total come out at 6,879. A symbol carrying `①` in Kanji mode is therefore reported as unmapped rather than decoded under a mapping the standard does not define.
- `EncodingModeExtensions.GetCountIndicatorLength` looked shared but encodes Standard QR's version thresholds (10/27); Micro QR and rMQR define their own indicator-width tables. The enum is shared; the width logic is per-symbology.
- The character-class predicates and alphanumeric encoding values (`IsNumeric`, `IsAlphanumeric`, `GetAlphanumericValue`, `IsValidISO88591`) lived inside the Standard QR constants class, so `TextAnalyzer` (shared) silently depended on the Standard QR table class. Applying the namespace dependency rule surfaced this immediately; the predicates now live in shared `CharacterSets`, the alphabets are identical across ISO/IEC 18004 and ISO/IEC 23941.
- **A UTF-16 code unit compared as `Int16` is negative above U+7FFF.** `TextAnalyzer`'s AVX2 and SSE2 tiers tested the ASCII (> 127) and ISO-8859-1 (> 255) thresholds with signed packed compares, so every char from U+8000 up — surrogate halves, meaning any emoji or other non-BMP char, plus U+FFFD and the CJK compatibility area — read as in range. Auto-detection then declared Latin-1 for text ISO-8859-1 cannot represent, and the Byte-mode Latin-1 writer truncated it (its own SSE2 tier saturates instead, so the corruption differed per architecture). The ARM64 tier was correct by construction: its reduction is `UMAXV`, unsigned. Two lessons. Threshold tests on char data must be unsigned, and at these two thresholds a bit test is both correct and cheaper than any compare (`c > 127` is "any bit from bit 7 up", `c > 255` is "any high-byte bit", one `vptest` on AVX2). And a tier the dispatcher cannot reach on the test machine needs a direct-entry parity test: AVX2 hides SSE2 on every CPU that has it, so the dispatch-level test cannot see an SSE2-only defect — `TextAnalyzerX64ParityTest` calls both entry points itself, the way the ARM64 test always has.

- **The core was never dependency-free on netstandard; SkiaSharp was hiding it.** `Span<T>`, `ArrayPool<T>` and `Unsafe` arrived through SkiaSharp's own dependency on `System.Memory` and `System.Runtime.CompilerServices.Unsafe`. Removing SkiaSharp broke only the netstandard2.0 and 2.1 builds, with 170 errors and nothing on net8.0+. The shims are referenced explicitly now, at the versions SkiaSharp pins, so a consumer of both packages resolves one copy. "Zero dependencies" is a statement about net8.0 and net10.0 and means "BCL shims only" on netstandard, and every document that uses the phrase says so.
- **Removing a dependency is a `using` audit.** The library had zero `using SkiaSharp;` lines because the root namespace `SkiaSharp.QrCode` resolved every `SK*` type implicitly; so did the tests (`SkiaSharp.QrCode.Tests`), the Playground (`SkiaSharp.QrCode.Playground`) and the Benchmark. Every namespace move surfaced the hidden imports as compile errors, once in Phase 1 for the library and again in Phase 4 for the Playground, and then IDE0005 pointed at the usings that had become redundant.
- **`CentralPackageTransitivePinningEnabled` rewrites nuspecs.** It promotes every pinned transitive package into a direct dependency of a packed project (for 1.x, the SkiaSharp native assets beside SkiaSharp). Nothing a consumer resolves changed when it was turned off, which is the proof that the promotion was a declaration, never a dependency; it is off repository-wide (see "Package graph").
- **C# 14 extension blocks emit public nested marker types** (`<G>$hash`, `<M>$hash`) that metadata readers and reflection both see. They broke the documentation trimmer, the shipped-documentation test and the approved-API listing at once. The rule everywhere is to skip nested types with an unspeakable name; the members themselves list on the enclosing class, which is what a caller writes.
- **A guard needs a negative test.** The nupkg dependency assertion passed on its first run; fed the shipped 1.1.1 package it produced four errors, which is the cheapest possible falsification and the one every future artifact-level check should repeat.
- **Two assemblies through one reflection tool means two PDBs and two XML files that overlap.** PolySharp emits the same documented polyfills into both, so a naive dictionary merge throws on the first shared key; exported types never collide, so first-wins is correct.
- **A seam needs its own contract tests, not the kernel's.** The luminance tier-parity tests proved the tiers agree with each other; nothing proved what the bytes mean until the BT.601 formula and the white compositing were written into a test. That test caught its own author's wrong assumption (all-zero bytes with an alpha channel are transparent, so white, not black), which is exactly the error a hand-written converter makes, and is why the `TryDecodeImage` documentation states the rule.
- **"Writable against the public surface" has two readings.** A third-party adapter can decode through `TryDecodeImage` and render through `GetModuleRectangles`; what it cannot get is the first-party fast path. The plan read the phrase as the second and published the luminance kernels; the maintainer's rule is the first (the public surface grows on request, not on anticipation, because an API is added in a minor and removed only in a major), and the kernels went back to internal. Build the rendering project with the `InternalsVisibleTo` grant removed to get the exact list of what it still reaches; reading produced a list one third the size.
- **Product name, package ID and repository URL are three strings that used to be one.** After the rename `FeatherQR` is the product, `SkiaSharp.QrCode` survives only as the metapackage ID, and the repository URL changed last. The mechanical rewrite worked only with a lookbehind for the repository owner and a lookahead for dotted project names; the header and installation blocks of the README were written by hand.
- **GitHub Pages project sites do not follow a repository rename**, and shared Playground links carry their settings in the URL hash, which a meta refresh drops. The user-site stub therefore forwards by script and keeps the meta refresh only as the no-script fallback. `user.github.io/<name>/` resolves to the project site first and the user site's folder second, so the stub is invisible until the project site is gone, which is expected rather than a deployment failure.
- **Transitive pinning, a file-based tool and a rename each have a blast radius the plan underestimated.** The plan's Phase 1 inventory expected one `InternalsVisibleTo` use and found three; expected zero core dependencies and found the netstandard shims; expected the dependency assertion to be a literal table and had to decide the pinning question first. Each was caught by a check that ran against the artifact rather than the source: the metadata test, the nupkg guard, the compiler with the grant removed.
